'''''Platanus racemosa''''' is a species of [[plane tree]] known by several common names, including '''California sycamore''', '''western sycamore''', '''California plane tree''', and in North American Spanish '''{{lang|es|aliso}}'''.<ref name="deardorff" /> ''Platanus racemosa''  is native to [[California]] and [[Baja California]], where it grows in [[riparian]] areas, [[canyon]]s, [[floodplain]]s, at [[Spring (hydrosphere)|springs]] and [[Seep (hydrology)|seeps]], and along [[stream]]s and [[river]]s in several types of [[habitat]]s.<ref name="deardorff">{{Cite journal|last=Deardorff|first=David|date=1977|title=Plant Portraits: California Sycamore (Platanus racemosa)|url=https://archive.org/stream/mobot31753004065816#page/4/mode/2up|journal=Garden|volume=1|pages=5–7|via=Archive.org}}</ref><ref name="samonps">Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area (N.R.A.), General Management Plan (GMP): Environmental Impact Statement. United States: n.p., 1982.</ref><ref>[https://www.nps.gov/samo/learn/nature/riparian-woodland.htm National Park Service Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area - Riparian Woodlands] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518151119/https://www.nps.gov/samo/learn/nature/riparian-woodland.htm |date=2021-05-18 }}. U.S. National Park Service</ref> It can be found as far north as [[Tehama County, California|Tehama]] and [[Humboldt County, California|Humboldt]] counties.  

==Description==
This large tree grows to {{Convert|35|m|ft|sigfig=2|sp=us}} in height with a trunk diameter of up to one meter (three feet). The height of these trees ranges from {{convert|10 to 35|m|sp=us}}.<ref name="Johnson-2016">{{Cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Matthew G. |last2=Lang |first2=Kylene |last3=Manos |first3=Paul |last4=Golet |first4=Greg H. |last5=Schierenbeck |first5=Kristina A. |date=2016-06-01 |title=Evidence for genetic erosion of a California native tree, Platanus racemosa, via recent, ongoing introgressive hybridization with an introduced ornamental species |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10592-015-0808-z |journal=Conservation Genetics |language=en |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=593–602 |doi=10.1007/s10592-015-0808-z |bibcode=2016ConG...17..593J |s2cid=254422699 |issn=1572-9737|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A specimen on the campus of [[Stanford University]] has a trunk girth (circumference) of {{Convert|10.5|ft|m|sigfig=3}}.<ref name="Stanford Trees">{{Cite web |url=http://trees.stanford.edu/ENCYC/PLATrac.htm |title=Stanford Trees, Shrubs, and Vines |access-date=2010-02-18 |archive-date=2010-07-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100713231728/http://trees.stanford.edu/ENCYC/PLATrac.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> The trunk generally divides into two or more large trunks splitting into many branches. The bark is an attractive patchwork of white, tawny beige, pinkish gray, and pale brown.<ref name="Peattie-1991" /> Both older bark and twigs on this plane sycamore become darker with time. The twigs and bark range from a light brownish gray to a shade resembling the color sepia.

''Platanus racemosa'' is the dominant species in the globally and state endangered [[Sycamore Alluvial Woodland|sycamore-alluvial woodland]] habitat.

The large [[Leaf shape|palmately lobed]] [[leaves]] may be up to {{Convert|25|cm|in|sigfig=2}} centimeters wide and have three or five pointed lobes.<ref name="Johnson-2016" /> New leaves are a bright translucent green and somewhat woolly.<ref name="Stanford Trees" /> The [[deciduous]] tree drops copious amounts of dry golden to orangish red leaves in the fall. The [[inflorescence]] is made up of a few spherical flower heads each around a centimeter wide.  The female flower heads develop into spherical fruit clusters each made up of many hairy, maroon-red-woolly [[achene]]s.<ref name="deardorff" /> Depending on the sex, the [[inflorescence]] can either be red, if female, or chartreuse, if male. After the female clusters fertilize, the achenes bear a fruit that breaks apart and scatters just as the tree's pollen does.<ref name="deardorff" /><ref name="Peattie-1991">{{Cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LfH16XDaVSkC&q=Platanus+racemosa&pg=PR7 |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |date=1991 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |isbn=978-0-395-58175-9 |language=en}}</ref>

The tough and coarse-grained wood is difficult to split and work. It has various uses, including acting as a meat preparation block for [[butchers]]. Many small birds feed on its fruit, and several mammals eat its twigs and bark. The [[pollen]] resulting from the hairs on the leaves and flowers of Western sycamores can be [[allergen]]s for some people.<ref name=cal>{{Cite web |url=http://www.californiagardens.com/Plant_Pages/platanus_racemosa.htm |title=Californiagardens.com |access-date=2010-02-18 |archive-date=2010-02-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100211131222/http://www.californiagardens.com/Plant_Pages/platanus_racemosa.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> New leaves are susceptible to [[Canker|anthracnose canker]], which, when it causes a side bud to become the new leader, can create picturesque angling trunks and branches on older specimens.<ref name=cal/><gallery>

==Cultivation==
It is also widely planted horticulturally as a [[ornamental plant|landscape tree]] in public landscapes and private gardens. While it requires some water, and can be grown in lawns, once established it is drought tolerant. New appreciation for how it shades sun in summer and lets sun through in winter has led to its use in [[green architecture]] and [[sustainable design]].

== Uses ==
California sycamore wood is extremely hard and difficult to work, but can still be employed to create a variety of items such as [[button]]s, tobacco boxes, furniture, wooden utensils, and barrels.<ref name="deardorff" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brush |first=Warren D. |date=December 1917 |title=Distinguishing Characters of North American Sycamore Woods |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/332176 |journal=Botanical Gazette |language=en |volume=64 |issue=6 |pages=480–496 |doi=10.1086/332176 |s2cid=84936560 |issn=0006-8071}}</ref> The form and wide canopy of the species make it an effective shade tree.<ref name="Peattie-1991" /> This western sycamore's shade cools the surrounding bodies of water while simultaneously offering a home for some animals in the humid environment in which it flourishes.<ref name="Lang">{{Cite web |last=Lang |first=Kylene R. |title=Microsatellite Development in "Plantanus" for Documenting Gene Flow Among Species |url=https://scholarworks.calstate.edu/concern/theses/8049g5613 |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=scholarworks.calstate.edu |language=English}}</ref> The Native [[Tongva]] people call the tree '''Shavar''', and teas prepared from its bark were traditionally used as a blood tonic, a remedy for asthma, and an aid during childbirth.<ref>{{cite web |title=Native Plants of the Baldwin Hills Scenic Overlook |url=https://www.parks.ca.gov/pages/612/files/Native_Plants_of_the_Baldwin_Hills_Scenic_Overlook.pdf |website=California State Parks.gov}}</ref> 

== Ecology ==
[[File:Sunol Preserve Platanus Racemosa.jpg|thumb|Wild California sycamore at Sunol Regional Wilderness]]
Increased human interference has made ''P. racemosa'' more susceptible to cross-breeding with other ''Platanus'' species. This [[Hybridization (biology)|hybridization]] with other species like ''P. x hispanica'' offers ''P. racemosa'' the advantage of resisting [[fungal diseases]], namely sycamore anthracnose. Interbred California sycamores are less vulnerable to this disease than the original ''P. racemosa'' as it harms their wood. However, sycamore anthracnose produces deadwood which creates a habitat for animals like [[wood duck]]s. The lack of non-hybridized ''P. racemosa'' thus harms the [[Riparian forest|riparian woodlands]] in which they thrive.<ref name="Lang" />

Another disease that ''P. racemosa'' is particularly receptive to is [[Fusarium]] dieback which is carried and passed on through two kinds of [[Invasive species|invasive]] [[ambrosia beetle]]s. Removing the tree itself is one way to prevent the significant harms of Fusarium dieback from spreading but a mixture of [[fungicide]]s such as metconazole combined with an [[insecticide]] can additionally reduce the number of ambrosia beetles that transmit this disease. Close monitoring is required in order to prevent a substantial beetle [[infestation]] from occurring as that would damage the tree to the point of needing removal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mayorquin |first1=Joey S. |last2=Carrillo |first2=Joseph D. |last3=Twizeyimana |first3=Mathias |last4=Peacock |first4=Beth B. |last5=Sugino |first5=Kameron Y. |last6=Na |first6=Francis |last7=Wang |first7=Danny H. |last8=Kabashima |first8=John N. |last9=Eskalen |first9=Akif |date=July 2018 |title=Chemical Management of Invasive Shot Hole Borer and Fusarium Dieback in California Sycamore ( Platanus racemosa ) in Southern California |journal=Plant Disease |language=en |volume=102 |issue=7 |pages=1307–1315 |doi=10.1094/PDIS-10-17-1569-RE |pmid=30673581 |bibcode=2018PlDis.102.1307M |issn=0191-2917|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Johnson-2016" />

Further hybridization between ''P. racemosa'' and ''P. x hispanica'' are a threat to the genetic diversity and identity of the former. The disease combatant advantage that the hybrid provides can bring about a decline in the native tree. The ensuing decline and genetic disintegration could not only harm the tree itself, but nesting birds, [[Monarch butterfly|monarch butterflies]], and numerous other small animals that reside or find shelter within the California sycamore's shade. D. Whitlock's study on the [[RNA]] of the ''Platanus'' trees near the [[Sacramento River]] reveals that ''P. racemosa'' contains [[gene]]s from ''P. x hispanica,'' which consequently demonstrates the increased erasure of the former.<ref name="Johnson-2016" />
